If your child is applying to an independent or private school, you will probably meet two tests: the **ISEE** and the **SSAT**. They measure similar skills, and many schools accept either one. They differ in ways that matter on test day, though: how levels are assigned, what the verbal section looks like, and how wrong answers are scored.

This guide explains the differences in plain English and ends with a simple plan for choosing and preparing.

## Step one: ask the schools

Before comparing anything, check the admissions page of every school on your list. Some schools accept only one test; many accept both. If every school accepts both, use the rest of this guide to pick the test that suits your child.

Both tests are now run by the same organization. The two former test owners, ERB (ISEE) and EMA (SSAT), merged into a nonprofit called **E3n**, and registration for both tests now happens through [admission.org](https://admission.org). You will still see the old names on older guides and score reports.

## The ISEE at a glance

The ISEE has four levels: **Primary** (applying to Grades 2–4), **Lower** (Grades 5–6), **Middle** (Grades 7–8) and **Upper** (Grades 9–12).

- **The level depends on the grade your child is applying to**, not their current grade. This is the most common registration mistake.
- **Primary levels** (2, 3 and 4) have only two multiple-choice sections: Reading and Mathematics. Primary 2 also has a few listening questions read aloud. There is no writing sample at the Primary levels.
- **Lower, Middle and Upper levels** have four scored multiple-choice sections: Verbal Reasoning, Quantitative Reasoning, Reading Comprehension and Mathematics Achievement. They also include an essay, which is sent to schools but not scored.
- **No penalty for guessing.** Wrong answers do not cost points, so students should answer every question.
- **Retakes are limited.** A student can take the ISEE once per testing season (fall, winter, spring and summer).

## The SSAT at a glance

The SSAT has three levels: **Elementary** (students currently in Grades 3–4), **Middle** (Grades 5–7) and **Upper** (Grades 8–11).

- **The level depends on the grade your child is in now.** This is the opposite of the ISEE rule.
- **Sections:** Quantitative (two math sections at Middle and Upper, one at Elementary), Reading, Verbal, an unscored writing sample and, at Middle and Upper, an unscored experimental section.
- **The verbal section is pure vocabulary:** synonyms and analogies. There are no sentence-completion questions.
- **Wrong answers cost a quarter point** at the Middle and Upper levels, so random guessing can lower a score. Students should guess only when they can rule out at least one choice.
- **More test dates.** Standard paper tests run on Saturdays through the year, and there are also Flex, Prometric and at-home options.

## Side-by-side comparison

| | ISEE | SSAT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Levels | Primary 2–4, Lower, Middle, Upper | Elementary, Middle, Upper |
| Level is based on | Grade applying to | Current grade |
| Verbal questions | Synonyms + sentence completion | Synonyms + analogies |
| Math | Two sections: reasoning + achievement | Two quantitative sections (one at Elementary) |
| Wrong answers | No penalty | Quarter-point penalty (Middle, Upper) |
| Essay | Unscored, sent to schools | Unscored, sent to schools |
| Retakes | Once per testing season | Several dates per year |

## Which one should your child take?

If the schools accept both, these patterns help:

- **Strong reader who enjoys word puzzles:** the SSAT's analogies reward students who like spotting relationships ("glove is to hand as sock is to foot").
- **Careful student who struggles with time pressure or guessing:** the ISEE's no-penalty scoring is more forgiving.
- **Strong in math concepts:** the ISEE's separate reasoning and achievement sections give more room to show math knowledge.
- **Needs flexible dates:** the SSAT usually offers more options.

The best way to decide is to have your child try a short official practice section of each test, then talk about which one felt better. Score percentiles compare students only with others in the same grade, so a "hard" test does not mean a lower result.

## Vocabulary is the common thread

Whichever test your child takes, vocabulary drives a big share of the verbal and reading score. Synonyms, sentence completions and analogies all depend on knowing what words mean, and reading passages are much easier when no word on the page is unfamiliar.

A steady routine works better than cramming:

1. **Learn 10–15 new words a day,** five days a week. That adds up to more than 600 words in three months.
2. **Review missed words** two days later and again a week later.
3. **Use the words in sentences** out loud. Saying a word in context helps it stick.
4. **Practice the question type** for your test: analogies for the SSAT, sentence completion for the ISEE.
